Caribbean & Mexico

The Right Island
Changes Everything.

The Caribbean and Mexico contain some of the finest beach and resort experiences in the world — and some of the most disappointing. The islands look similar on a map and in photographs. On the ground, the differences between them are the whole trip. Getting this right starts before the booking.

Plan a Caribbean Trip Explore Destinations ↓
Best Season
December – April
The Region

Not All Sand and Blue
Water Is the Same

Peak season runs December through April, when the weather is most reliable and rates are highest; hurricane season runs July to October. Most trips run 5–8 days. The island decides more than the resort does: St. Barth's is small, expensive and Parisian with no chain hotels, Turks and Caicos is about water clarity, and the Riviera Maya adds cenotes and Mayan sites.

Turks & Caicos and the Dominican Republic are both Caribbean. The water in both is warm. The sand in both is white. The experience in both is categorically different — and the price difference between the two is not always what travelers assume it will be. St. Barth's is expensive because it is genuinely exclusive and genuinely exceptional. Jamaica at the right property in the right parish is one of the most culturally rich experiences in the region. Los Cabos in Mexico is a desert peninsula meeting the Pacific where the right villa community and the right time of year produces something that no all-inclusive can approach.

The planning work in this region is more consequential than almost anywhere else because the stakes are higher and the surface-level research is more misleading. Photos of turquoise water and white sand look identical across a dozen islands with very different realities. The right question is never which island — it's which property, which room category, which month, and which version of the destination you're actually looking for.

We've been planning Caribbean and Mexico travel long enough to know the properties that deliver, the islands that have earned their reputation, and the months that make or break a trip. The research doesn't start at the destination — it starts with understanding exactly what kind of trip you're trying to have.

Where We Send Clients

Six Destinations Worth Planning Properly

Each has a version that photographs well and a version that actually delivers. The difference is in the details — property, timing, room category, and what you're actually there for.

British West Indies
Turks & Caicos
Grace Bay Beach ranks among the finest in the world, and the ranking is accurate — twelve miles of uninterrupted white sand. The island is small enough to navigate without a car and uncrowded even at peak season. North shore villas give families the space resort rooms cannot. Best December through April.
Grace Bay Private Villas Water Sports

French West Indies
St. Barth's
The most genuinely exclusive island in the Caribbean — small, French, with an airport approach that needs a pilot who has done it before. A villa is the right way to see it: private pool, provisioned kitchen, a hillside terrace above Gustavia. Best December through March, and quieter still in May.
Private VillasFrench CaribbeanGustavia

Destination Photography · Jamaica
Greater Antilles
Jamaica
The most culturally specific island in the Caribbean, with its own music, its own food tradition, its own way of conducting time. Boutique all-inclusives on the western cliffs, the Blue Mountains in the east, a jerk chicken lunch the hotel guide knows by name. Skip the mega-resorts near Montego Bay.
Blue MountainsFoodBoutique Resorts
Explore →
Destination Photography · Eastern Caribbean
Eastern Caribbean
Barbados & Eastern Caribbean
Barbados for the Platinum Coast — properties that have done luxury correctly for decades, and a food scene that outperforms the island's size. St. Lucia for the Pitons and a volcanic landscape no flat island replicates. Antigua and Anguilla for sailors who know the right island at the right time.
BarbadosSt. Lucia PitonsAnguilla
Explore →
Mexico
Riviera Maya & Los Cabos
Two very different versions of Mexico. Riviera Maya for the cenotes, the Tulum ruins, and adults-only properties in the jungle that bear no resemblance to the hotel zone. Los Cabos for the desert peninsula where the Pacific meets the Sea of Cortez. Both reward the same approach: skip the resorts.
Riviera MayaLos CabosTulum

Greater Antilles
Dominican Republic
The most value-dense destination in the Caribbean when planned properly — not the hotel zone near Punta Cana, but the boutique all-inclusives at Las Terrenas on the Samaná Peninsula, the golf at Casa de Campo, and the north coast near Cabarete, where the kite-surfing is genuinely world class.

Featured Itineraries

Trips We Plan Often

Caribbean and Mexico itineraries built around the access and specificity that makes the region deliver — not just the destination, but the right version of it.

Itinerary Photography
Grace Bay · Turks & Caicos
December – April · 6–8 days
Turks & Caicos Villa Week
A north-shore villa on Providenciales — three or four bedrooms, a private pool, and a chef who comes in four evenings and leaves the kitchen provisioned for the others. Mornings on Grace Bay, where the water is shallow enough to walk for a quarter mile and clear enough to read the sand patterns at ten feet depth. An afternoon boat charter to the uninhabited cays for a snorkel over the barrier reef and a sundowner on a sandbar that disappears at high tide. Two dinners at the island's best restaurant, where the reservation matters and the fish came in that morning. A week that most clients come back from saying they didn't realize the Caribbean could be that quiet.
Turks & Caicos6–8 Days

Villa Community · Los Cabos
October – May · 5–7 days
Los Cabos Private Villa & Pacific Coast
A private villa in one of the gated communities between San José del Cabo and Cabo San Lucas — the ones with direct beach access, a private pool, and staff who have been with the property for a decade. An early morning deep-sea fishing charter out of the marina, chasing marlin and dorado on the Pacific side where the cold Humboldt Current meets the warm Sea of Cortez. An afternoon taco tour through San José del Cabo's art district, a market lunch at a tortillería that opens at seven and closes when the tortillas run out, and a dinner at a rooftop restaurant that requires knowing the chef is actually in the kitchen that night.

Itinerary Photography
Jungle Boutique · Riviera Maya
November – April · 6–8 days
Riviera Maya Adults Escape
Four nights at a boutique adults-only property outside Tulum — no swim-up bar, no entertainment schedule, a palapa roof and a cenote on the grounds that guests share with the local wildlife. A morning at the Tulum ruins before the buses arrive, when the Mayan temple sits above the Caribbean with nothing between it and the sea. An afternoon at a backcountry cenote accessible only by local guide, swimming through a cave formation in water that is fifty-five degrees and perfectly clear. Two nights in Playa del Carmen for contrast — the Fifth Avenue food scene, a dive morning on the reef, and a beach club sunset that doesn't require pretending you're somewhere else.

Cliff Terrace · St. Barth's
December – April · 5–7 days
St. Barth's High Season
A hillside villa overlooking Gustavia harbor — a private pool, a kitchen provisioned by the island's best grocery and a chef for three evenings, and a terrace where the view at sunset genuinely justifies the rate. A morning at St. Jean Beach before the day visitors arrive. A harbor lunch at a French bistro where the moules marinières are the same as they were in 1978 and nobody rushes the table. An afternoon boat excursion around the north coast to the uninhabited beaches that can only be reached by water. Gustavia for the evening — a rum punch on a dock, a dinner that starts at nine, and a night that ends when it feels like it should. The island that clients who've been everywhere come back to every year.

Why Plan With Us

What We Add to Caribbean & Mexico Travel

The Caribbean and Mexico look simple to book. The detail work that separates a good trip from a forgettable one is less obvious here than almost anywhere — and more consequential when it goes wrong.

⬡
Property Curation
The Caribbean has more luxury-priced hotels per square mile than almost any region in the world — and the quality range at similar price points is enormous. We know which properties actually deliver the rate, which villas have the right staff ratio, and which all-inclusives have earned the designation through food quality and access rather than amenity lists.
⬡
Room Category Guidance
At most Caribbean resorts, room category is the single most consequential booking decision — more than date, more than length of stay. The difference between a garden-view room and a beachfront suite at the same property is frequently the difference between a good trip and an exceptional one. We don't book the room that fits the budget without making sure it fits the trip.
⬡
Virtuoso Partner Access
Preferred partner rates, suite upgrades, resort credits, and early check-in at participating Caribbean and Mexico properties through our Virtuoso membership. At properties like the top Turks & Caicos resorts and the major Los Cabos hotels, the amenity package frequently offsets the planning fee entirely — and the reservation carries more weight than a direct booking.
⬡
Seasonal & Weather Guidance
Hurricane season in the Caribbean runs June through November, with the highest risk in September and October. Most travelers know this and still book into the window thinking odds are on their side. We advise on the actual risk profile by island, the insurance options worth carrying, and the windows that deliver the same pricing without the exposure — most of which fall in May, early June, and late November.
When to Go

Caribbean & Mexico by Season

Peak Season
December – April
The primary Caribbean and Mexico window — dry, calm, and consistently excellent across every destination in the region. Christmas and New Year's are the most expensive two weeks of the year; January through March offers the same weather at meaningfully lower rates. Top properties at Turks & Caicos and St. Barth's book out six months in advance for February. Book early.
Best Overall Window
Summer
June – August
The Caribbean in summer is warmer, more humid, and cheaper — meaningfully so. The water remains excellent. School-holiday timing makes June and July the primary family window despite the heat. Los Cabos in summer is one of the best value propositions in the region — the Pacific side stays cooler than the Caribbean, hotel rates drop significantly, and the fishing season peaks for marlin and dorado. Hurricane risk is present but typically low before September.
Shoulder & Off-Season
May & November
The two best-kept secrets in Caribbean travel. May is post-peak and pre-hurricane — rates are 30–40% lower than February, weather is excellent, and the islands are noticeably quieter. Late November after Thanksgiving is similar: the peak-season machine is warming up, but rates haven't caught up yet. September and October carry genuine hurricane risk and are not recommended for travel to the Caribbean without comprehensive travel insurance and flexible dates.

Common Questions

Caribbean & Mexico — FAQ

Questions about island selection, hurricane season, resort choices, and how to build a trip that goes beyond the standard package.

Significant. St. Barts is small, private, and Parisian in character — expensive, no chain hotels, excellent food. Turks and Caicos is about beaches and water clarity — some of the clearest in the world — with limited cultural activity. Jamaica has music, food culture, and character alongside strong resort options. St. Lucia is scenically dramatic. Barbados blends English heritage with a sophisticated dining scene. The right island depends entirely on what you want the trip to feel like.

Officially June 1 through November 30, with the highest-risk period typically August–October. Many travelers book July–November at lower rates, accepting a small but real probability of disruption. Islands south of the traditional hurricane belt — Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao, Trinidad — carry meaningfully lower risk. Travel insurance during this window is strongly advisable.

Los Cabos has the deepest inventory of luxury hotels at the tip of Baja California. The Corridor has produced some of Mexico's most design-forward properties. Riviera Maya (Tulum through Playa del Carmen) offers both ultra-luxury boutique options and family-friendly all-inclusive resorts. Puerto Vallarta and Punta Mita deliver a more authentically Mexican character with world-class resort options.

Yes — inter-island flights make this manageable. Popular combinations include Turks and Caicos with the Bahamas, Barbados with St. Lucia, or a broader Eastern Caribbean island hop. Adding Havana or San Juan as a city anchor works well. I design multi-island itineraries around how each destination complements the others in pace, character, and activity.

Different experiences. The Riviera Maya has proximity to Mayan ruins (Chichen Itza, Tulum, Cobá), cenotes, and deeper cultural context alongside its resorts. Los Cabos is more resort-focused, with dramatic desert-meets-ocean scenery, excellent sport fishing, and some of Mexico's finest luxury properties. The right choice depends on whether you want cultural depth or pure resort experience.

The all-inclusive model removes billing friction and works well when you plan to stay on-property most of the time. Independent resorts give more flexibility and often deliver better food and more individualized service. At the top end, the distinction narrows significantly. I advise based on your travel style and what you actually want from the trip, not a blanket preference for one model.

St. Barts, Turks and Caicos, and St. Lucia are the three I recommend most often for honeymoons. St. Barts for privacy, sophistication, and food. Turks for the beach and water quality. St. Lucia for dramatic scenery, a sense of place, and a combination of activity and relaxation. The right answer depends on your budget and what you value most in a honeymoon experience.

US citizens traveling to Mexico and most Caribbean destinations require a valid US passport for reentry. A passport card works for some land and sea crossings but not air travel. US territories (Puerto Rico, USVI) don't require a passport for US citizens. Entry requirements for non-US travelers vary by destination. I verify requirements for every client and flag any documentation that needs advance preparation.
